chunks.content: 96 The One Due Diligence Mistake That Could Tank Your Business Acquisition Hi Sara, Buying a business? You’re probably knee-deep in financial statements, debt service coverage ratios, and making sure the numbers check out. But do you know what most buyers completely ignore? The employee handbook. Yes, that legally questionable 70-page document no one—including the seller—has ever actually read. And yet, skipping it nearly torpedoed a deal I worked on last week. The Landmine Hiding in Plain Sight A buyer was acquiring a small business—just five employees, all women. Everyone was excited. I casually asked for the employment handbook, mostly as a formality. They sent it over as a joke, like, “Sure, if you really want to waste your time.” Well, guess what I found? The seller had unknowingly adopted big-company policies (think FMLA, ADA) that didn’t even apply to them. Buried in the fine print? A 12-week paid maternity leave policy—which the seller had no idea existed. The five employees? They definitely knew. Now the buyer had a tough choice: ➝ Match the policy and take a financial hit. ➝ Cut it and risk losing the entire team post-close. Oh, and they weren’t allowed to talk to employees before closing—so they had to make the call blind. Why This Matters (Even in an Asset Purchase) "It’s an asset purchase—I’m not taking on liabilities, so who cares?" Because you’re not just buying assets, you’re buying people. Employees don’t magically reset their expectations just because ownership changes hands. If you don’t honor policies they were promised, they’ll leave. What You Should Be Checking (That You’re Probably Not) ➝ The employee handbook (yes, really—just skim it). ➝ Hidden liabilities in PTO, benefits, or outdated workplace policies that could become your problem. ➝ Anything that might make employees feel like they got a raw deal when you take over. Most buyers only realize this after key employees start quitting—or when they find themselves stuck with unexpected financial obligations. Don’t be that buyer. If you want to avoid post-close chaos, check out our courses on Deal Academy for expert guidance on running a smooth diligence process. To deals that don’t implode, Sara Sharp Partner, SK&S Law Group Business Consultant & Founder of Deal Academy P.S.
